title: The best direction is an eigenvector
summary: The eigenvector of C with the largest eigenvalue spreads the points most, and its line is the closest to them.

blocks.title: The eigenvalues of C

define.meaning: A non-zero $v$ with $Cv = \lambda v$: $C$ only stretches it, by the eigenvalue $\lambda$.

blocks.why: The best direction will turn out to be an eigenvector of $C$, and its variance an eigenvalue. Find the eigenvalues first.

slips.say: Those are the eigenvalues of $X^\mathsf{T}X = 4C$. Divide by $n - 1$, or work with $C$ itself.

hints: The eigenvalues add up to the trace ($7 + 4$) and multiply to the determinant.

check.say: They should add up to 11, your total variance.

blocks.solution: 8 is the variance your best guess reached. That is not a coincidence.

blocks.title: v₁
blocks.why: $v_1$, the unit eigenvector for the largest eigenvalue, is the candidate for the best direction.
blocks.prompt: Find $v_1$, the unit eigenvector of $C$ for $\lambda_1 = 8$.

answer.acceptNote: Either sign is right: $-v_1$ is the same line.

slips.say: The right direction. Now make it a unit vector: divide by its length.

hints: So $x = 2y$: the direction is $(2, 1)$, and its length is $\sqrt5$.

check.say: $C$ times $(2, 1)$ should be 8 times $(2, 1)$. Then check $x^2 + y^2 = 1$ for your unit vector.

blocks.solution: Your better guess from the first lesson. Next: why nothing beats it.
blocks.next: See why it is the best

blocks.title: Why nothing beats v₁

define.meaning: The unit eigenvector for $\lambda_2 = 3$. For a symmetric matrix, eigenvectors with different eigenvalues are perpendicular, so $v_1, v_2$ is a pair of perpendicular unit axes.

blocks.why: This turns "no guess got past 8" into a proof, for every direction at once.
blocks.prompt: Any unit $u$ is $a v_1 + b v_2$ with $a^2 + b^2 = 1$, and then $u^\mathsf{T}Cu = 8a^2 + 3b^2$. What is the largest $u^\mathsf{T}Cu$ can be?

slips.say: $8a^2 + 3b^2$ can't reach $8 + 3$: $a^2$ and $b^2$ share 1 between them.

hints: It is largest at $a^2 = 1$, $b = 0$: that is $u = \pm v_1$.

check.say: Try $a = b = 1/\sqrt2$: it should give something between 3 and 8.

blocks.solution: So the variance along $u$ is largest at $u = v_1$, and there it is $\lambda_1$. That is **principal component analysis (PCA)**: the first principal direction is the top eigenvector of $C$, and the variance along it is the top eigenvalue.

blocks.title: v₂
blocks.why: The second principal direction holds the spread that the first one misses.
blocks.prompt: Find $v_2$, the unit eigenvector of $C$ for $\lambda_2 = 3$. Take the one with a positive second entry.

answer.acceptNote: That is $-v_2$, the same line. Later lessons use $(-1, 2)/\sqrt5$.

slips.say: The right direction. Now make it a unit vector.

hints: It is perpendicular to $v_1$, which points along $(2, 1)$.

check.say: $v_1 \cdot v_2$ should be 0, and $C(-1, 2)$ should be $3 \cdot (-1, 2)$.

blocks.next: Measure the distance to the best line

blocks.title: The closest line
blocks.why: Least squares measured the distance from points to a line straight up. PCA's line is the best one measured straight to the line.
blocks.prompt: For the line through the mean along $v_1$, what is the mean squared distance from the points to it: the sum of squared perpendicular distances, divided by $n - 1$?

widget.name: pca-scatter
widget.caption: Show the best direction, then turn the line onto it: the variance along it peaks just as the distance to it bottoms out.

slips.say: That is the sum of squared distances. Now divide by $n - 1$.

hints: By Pythagoras, each point's squared distance to the line is $\|x_i\|^2 - (x_i \cdot v_1)^2$.
So the answer is the total variance minus the variance along $v_1$.

check.say: It should equal $\lambda_2$, the variance along $v_2$: the perpendicular drops are exactly each point's part along $v_2$.

blocks.solution: $\lambda_2 = 3$. Since along + across is always 11, the line with the most spread along it is the line closest to the points. It is not the least-squares line: least squares of $y$ on $x$ here has slope $\frac{8}{28} = \frac27$; PCA's line has slope $\frac12$.

sideQuest.title: Check it in numpy
sideQuest.body:
Only if you want to.

```
import numpy as np
C = np.array([[7, 2], [2, 4]])
values, vectors = np.linalg.eigh(C)  # eigh: for symmetric matrices, smallest first
print(values)   # [3. 8.]
print(vectors)  # columns are v2 and v1, each up to sign
```
